issues.legal_issue: A court may extend the time to pay a small deficit in a pre-emption decree when the shortfall resulted from a bona fide inadvertent mistake rather than negligence or inaction.
material_facts: The decree required payment of the purchase money by a specified deadline but described the amount by reference to a deduction that was not quantified in the decree.
The decree-holder deposited nearly all the amount before the deadline, but an inadvertent arithmetic error left a small deficit.
The court officials allowed the deposit application and accompanying challan without pointing out the shortfall, and possession was delivered to the decree-holder.
The decree-holder sought permission to deposit the deficit after it was discovered, and the trial court found sufficient cause to extend the time.
issues.conclusion: The trial court had discretion to extend the time under section 148 of the Code of Civil Procedure, even after the deadline had expired, because the small shortfall resulted from a bona fide inadvertent mistake and was not indicative of negligence or inaction.
issues.legal_principle: Order XX rule 14(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure makes dismissal mandatory when the required purchase money is not paid within the fixed time and there is no order justifying or excusing non-payment. However, section 148 gives the court discretion to enlarge a period it fixed, including after expiry, where a relatively small fraction was omitted through a bona fide mistake that does not indicate negligence or inaction. Where the mistake resulted from or was induced by the court’s own action, the maxim actus curiae neminem gravabit applies. The Court relied on Naguba Appa v. Namdev, Jogdhayan v. Babu Ram, Jang Singh v. Brijlal, and Labh Singh v. Hardayal.

rule.if: preemption_decree_proceeding and small_fraction_unpaid and inadvertent_bona_fide_mistake and not negligence_or_inaction

predicates.preemption_decree_proceeding: The proceeding involves a decree granting a claim to pre-emption and requiring payment of purchase money.
predicates.small_fraction_unpaid: The person required to pay deposited nearly all of the purchase money but left a relatively small fraction unpaid by the deadline.
predicates.inadvertent_bona_fide_mistake: The shortfall resulted from an unintended mistake made in good faith.
predicates.negligence_or_inaction: The shortfall was attributable to negligence or inaction by the person required to pay.

issues.definition: When a pre-emption decree requires payment and nearly all the purchase money was paid, a bona fide inadvertent shortfall without negligence or inaction permits the court to extend the payment time.

issues.legal_issue: A revisional court cannot set aside a trial court’s discretionary extension of time unless the trial court lacked jurisdiction or committed a material legal or procedural error.
material_facts: The trial court allowed the decree-holder additional time to pay the small deficit, exercising its discretion after finding sufficient cause.
The High Court set aside that order in revision, relying on its view that court officials had not caused the shortfall.
The trial court had authority to extend time under section 148, and no material breach of law or procedural error affecting the decision was established.
issues.conclusion: The High Court had no basis to interfere in revision with the trial court’s order, and the Supreme Court restored that order.
issues.legal_principle: Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits revision on jurisdictional grounds, including lack of jurisdiction, its irregular exercise or non-exercise, or its illegal assumption. A revisional court may interfere where the subordinate court lacked jurisdiction or breached a legal provision or committed a material procedural error that may have affected the ultimate decision; it may not interfere merely because it differs on fact or law. The Court relied on Keshardeo Chamria v. Radha Kissen Chamria. It also relied on section 148 and the principles stated in Mahanth Ram Das v. Ganga Das and Ganesh Prasad Sah Kesari v. Lakshmi Narayan Gupta concerning the court’s power to enlarge time.

predicates.revision_proceeding: A party has asked a higher court to revise a subordinate court’s order.
predicates.trial_court_had_authority_to_extend_time: The subordinate court had legal authority to make the order extending time.
predicates.material_jurisdictional_or_procedural_er: The subordinate court lacked jurisdiction or committed a material legal or procedural error that may have affected the outcome.

issues.definition: In a revision proceeding, where the trial court had authority to extend time and made no material jurisdictional or procedural error, the higher court cannot set aside its order merely because it disagrees with its reasoning.

issues.legal_issue: Filing an appeal does not itself suspend a pre-emption decree, although an appellate stay may suspend the decree to the extent and in the manner specified by the stay order.
material_facts: The Court considered the effect of an appeal and an appellate stay on the payment obligations imposed by a pre-emption decree.
It distinguished cases in which no appellate stay was granted from cases in which a stay affected performance of the decree’s reciprocal obligations.
The Court relied on decisions addressing the effect of appellate stays and whether a fresh period for payment was fixed or arose by implication.
issues.conclusion: An appeal alone does not suspend a pre-emption decree; an appellate stay can suspend it in the manner ordered, and its effect on payment obligations and any fresh payment period depends on the terms and effect of that order.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order XX rule 14(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, the decree’s payment condition remains operative unless an order of a court justifies or excuses non-payment. Filing an appeal does not itself suspend the decree. An appellate stay may suspend the reciprocal obligations under the decree to the extent provided by the order, and the court must examine whether the stay affects deemed dismissal and fixes or implies a fresh period for payment. The Court relied on Naguba Appa v. Namdev, Dattatraya v. Shaikh Mahboob Shaikh Ali, and Sulleh Singh v. Sohan Lal.

predicates.preemption_decree_on_appeal: A pre-emption decree is subject to an appeal.
predicates.appeal_filed_without_stay: An appeal has been filed but no appellate order stays the decree.
predicates.appellate_stay_granted: An appellate court has made an order staying the decree or its operation.

issues.definition: For a pre-emption decree under appeal, its operation remains in force if no stay was granted and is suspended only to the extent and in the manner provided by an appellate stay.
